quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results from the call: same-store revenue growth for the fourth quarter was 35% and quarterly gross margin exceeded 25% for the first time in company history (25.5% vs 23.2%; mechanical 24.9% vs 22.4%, electrical 26.9%). EPS was $9.37, up 129%, and full-year 2025 EPS was $28.88 versus $14.60 in 2024. Quarterly operating income rose 89% to $427,000,000 (16.1% of revenue vs 12.1%); EBITDA rose 78% to $464,000,000, and full-year 2025 EBITDA was $1,450,000,000 with a 16% margin.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 same-store revenue growth 35%; Q4 gross margin 25.5%; Q4 EPS $9.37 (+129%); 2025 EPS $28.88 vs $14.60; Q4 EBITDA $464,000,000 (+78%); 2025 EBITDA $1,450,000,000

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 bookings: same-store sequential backlog rose $2,400,000,000, or 26%, driven by technology-sector bookings in both traditional construction and modular, and more than one-half of the sequential increase was new modular bookings; with more modular and larger projects, backlog duration keeps extending. The CFO said a little over half of the $2,600,000,000 sequential increase in bookings was new modular bookings, and a huge proportion of that modular work will perform in 2027, some in 2026 in the new buildings and some in 2028; the well over a billion dollars of other new construction bookings are led by data centers, with manufacturing, pharma and food processing also active.
quarterly_data.figure: same-store sequential backlog +$2,400,000,000 (26%); sequential bookings increase $2,600,000,000, a little over half modular

quarterly_data.signal: Asked whether the backlog reflects the recent hyperscaler CapEx announcements, the CFO said Comfort is a late-cycle player: backlog requires a binding legal commitment, a price and a scope, so booked work is for buildings planned a year or two ago ('the holes have been dug'), and revenue reflects projects that came up one to two and a half years earlier. Commitments the hyperscalers are making now will show up in Comfort's revenue in 2027, 2028.

2025 revenue mix: industrial (which includes technology) was 67% of volume; technology, dominated by data center work, was 45% of revenue, up from 33% the prior year, and is the largest driver of pipeline and backlog; institutional 21%; construction 86% of revenue (new buildings 63%, existing buildings 23%); modular 18% of revenue; service revenue grew 12% to a record $1,200,000,000 and is now 14% of revenue. The CEO said advanced technology is 'overwhelmingly data center' and that good partners make it worth dedicating the overwhelming majority of Comfort's resources to that vertical; Texas (a combination of modular and stick build, where Comfort has the largest electrical contractor) is 'really probably unique in the country with the amount of build.'
quarterly_data.figure: technology 45% of revenue (vs 33%); industrial 67%; institutional 21%; construction 86%; modular 18%; service revenue $1,200,000,000 (+12%, 14% of revenue)

quarterly_data.signal: Modular capacity is currently around 3,000,000 square feet and is expected to reach approximately 4,000,000 square feet by the end of 2026, weighted to the first half; the single biggest space procurement closes in February and capacity comes online gradually over the year (final assembly space can be productive very quickly). The CFO said the expansion is 'primarily us taking steps to meet more of the demand from our two largest customers. They would buy more if they could' - the new floor space is planned for 'those two large hyperscaler customers'; a few other modular customers have been added, 'but none of them are at scale.'
quarterly_data.figure: modular capacity around 3,000,000 sq ft now; approximately 4,000,000 sq ft by end of 2026

quarterly_data.signal: 2025 CapEx was $155,000,000, just over 1.7% of revenues (modular capacity expansion and service vehicles). For 2026 the CFO called 1.7% a baseline rate, with building purchases on top - a $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 building moves the meter a couple tenths of a percent; one very large building purchase happens in the first quarter and another very big one, probably in North Carolina, is being evaluated for lease or purchase. Comfort prefers buying these buildings because of the robotics and automation it installs: 'you really do not want to drop $30,000,000 into a $60,000,000 building you do not own.'
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 CapEx $155,000,000 (just over 1.7% of revenues); 2026 baseline about 1.7% plus building purchases

quarterly_data.signal: Asked about possible changes to cooling requirements for next-generation chips, the CFO said the impact on Comfort is 'not at all': 'the new chip stuff—they said, okay, we can use 45-degree water. Still needs pipe. Still needs water.' He added that 45-degree water is not naturally occurring for 99% of the year in 99% of places, and that as long as servers run on electricity they produce heat, so customers will keep needing electricians and pipe fitters; the CEO said the change is 'Far more impactful for the OEMs than for us.'
quarterly_data.figure: 45-degree water (next-generation chip cooling requirement cited by management)

quarterly_data.signal: Construction capacity is scarce: the CFO said 'Not everybody who wants a building gets one,' and some Q4 bookings were customers trying to sign Comfort up for their projects as soon as possible. Labor is where Comfort takes all of its risk (there are no four-year price locks for labor); Comfort hires with an all-of-the-above approach plus its in-house traveling contract craft professionals (Kodiak and Pivot), has over 22,000 employees and says 'we have a lot of work to chase.' Scarcity lets it demand to be rewarded for risk and scarce resources; highly specified equipment is never quoted without a supplier quote, and customers release Comfort to buy equipment very early, sometimes before the work enters backlog. The CEO said the company stays disciplined: 'The work we have, we can handle.'

Initial 2026 outlook: management is optimistic that gross profit margins will continue in the strong ranges of the last several quarters, with the usual seasonally lower first quarter (January ice storms shut jobs at some of its biggest operations for multiple days), and estimates a 2026 tax rate of around 23%; SG&A (Q4 $248,000,000, 9.4% of revenue vs 11.1%) should grow more slowly than revenue. The analyst's question cites a 2026 same-store revenue growth expectation of mid to high teens, and the reply (printed inside the analyst's turn in this transcript) repeats 'mid to high teens,' says growth should be consistent through the year and that steeper second-half comparables, not first-half weighting, drive the pattern.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 tax rate around 23%; Q4 SG&A $248,000,000 (9.4% of revenue vs 11.1%)

quarterly_data.signal: 2025 operating cash flow was $1,200,000,000 and full-year free cash flow was a record $1,000,000,000. Comfort returned more than $200,000,000 to shareholders in 2025 by buying over 440,000 shares at an average price of $489; the CFO said two consecutive $0.10 dividend increases are almost a 50% increase, the M&A pipeline is good but 'the cash flow is relentless,' and Comfort is paying more for acquisitions than ever because a company with hundreds of electricians who have worked together for years is worth more.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 operating cash flow $1,200,000,000; free cash flow $1,000,000,000; more than $200,000,000 of buybacks (over 440,000 shares at $489)
